title: Stop Playing Small
author: Cindy Chance
summary: Executive coach and ethicist Cindy Chance opens with a confession: she used to throw herself into hopeless causes, convincing herself that important work justified being undermined and unsupported, and only later recognized this as a way of playing small. Her central argument is that the greatest risk to leaders is internal rather than external: many have lost, buried, or never cultivated a deep connection to themselves, and whatever they build (a family, a business, a team) will come to reflect what they are hiding from. She pairs a spiritual reading (something is always greater than fear) with a social-science one (fear takes higher-order thinking offline) to explain how fear and comfort keep people stuck. The practical move is to become curious and name one's own patterns, which she likens to removing paint from a window, and to treat challenge as opportunity. She closes with a friend's tenfold business goal to argue that big goals can be easier than small ones because they force leaders to change fundamental assumptions and become different people.
points: Chance reframes staying in doomed organizations and causes as a form of playing small, driven by an unexamined belief that feeling alone and undermined is the price of worthwhile work.
She argues leaders' unaddressed fears and patterns get reproduced in what they build, and they miss it because they are busy not seeing it in themselves.
People around a leader can feel whether that leader is fully present to themselves, so inner work is not merely private but shapes the way things go for others.
The first step out of playing small is curiosity: noticing and naming one's customary patterns creates a moment to substitute something more resonant.
Audacious goals can be easier than modest ones because incremental effort cannot achieve them, forcing leaders to revisit assumptions, recruit intimidating collaborators, and change internally.
quotes: What I should have been asking: when did you learn that feeling alone, undermined and unsupported was part of doing something worthwhile — and couldn’t your time, energy and talent be better spent elsewhere?

The real risk I see again and again in individuals and organizations is that individual leaders have lost, buried, or never cultivated a deep enough connection to themselves. Not being present to yourself creates all kinds of big problems.

Because whatever you are building will come to reflect what you are hiding from, in corresponding, visible ways. Whatever you are building. Your family. Your business. Your team. And you will not see it, because you are so busy not seeing it in yourself.

The spiritual way of looking at this: there is always something greater than fear. The social science way: fear runs our biology at the lowest level, taking our higher order thinking and feeling offline. Running on fear and comfort keeps you small.

When we start to see our own patterns, we begin to increase our power. There is a moment in the noticing when we can substitute whatever is our customary focus with something more resonant that pulls us to higher ground.

Here’s what she learned: big goals can be easier than small ones because they require us to change more. You cannot achieve big goals merely by working a little harder or being a little more tolerant of risk.
